newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Metal markets bubble behind rally in copper.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Metal markets bubble behind rally in copper.

text.p: An explosive rally in copper helped ignite price rises in other key industrial metals on Wednesday. Aluminium rose above $1,500 a tonne on the London Metal Exchange (LME) to hit $1,505 -- its highest for 2-1/2 months -- as consumers returned to that market. Investment funds bought zinc up to $1,085, its best for 6-1/2 months.
"Everything seems to be bubbling along led by copper," said Angus MacMillan, analyst at LME broker Billiton Metals Ltd.

Copper reached $2,240 a tonne, extending a rally that began late last week. Data suggesting that stocks are at their lowest for more than six years is largely behind the advance by copper, to its highest since June when it was hit by the Sumitomo Corp scandal and fell as low as $1,745.
A trader said this week's general advance in the metals sector "is mostly about good chart signals and speculators buying metal...all on the back of copper".
Aluminium gained $20 despite a report by the International Primary Aluminium Institute (IPAI) that average daily output by the major producers rose in August.
Because aluminium prices have been depressed for some time consumers have been buying only what they need for immediate requirements in what MacMillan called a hand-to-mouth policy.
But signs that the price had bottomed out and was starting to rise may have persuaded end-users to think again.
"We could see re-stocking and forward buying, and that is what is happening today," MacMillan said.
Meanwhile, speculators have been attracted to zinc, used in galvanising steel, by the twin signals of falling stocks and positive readings on technical charts, traders add.
Gains were made against the background of recent confirmation by Spanish zinc producer Asturiana de Zinc that it had offloaded a large long LME futures position.
Concerns about this position had been capping the zinc market throughout the last few years, with prices rarely able to shift away from the $1,000/tonne level despite gains elsewhere.
Analysts said rallies in aluminium, zinc and any other LME metal depend a lot on what takes place in copper.
Copper prices are being bouyed by very low visible stock levels and high cash premiums, with the market also buffeted by big speculative swings that are a legacy of the Sumitomo affair.

Copper is at its highest since June 14 when Sumitomo sacked star trader Yasuo Hamanaka. It alleged that Hamanaka, the architect of a high price copper trading strategy, was a maverick who lost it $2.6 billion in unauthorized deals. Conditions in copper are nervous and volatile, resulting in rapid price moves.
"Nobody can call the next $200 move," MacMillan said.
